Topic: Is it not a deeper theft to inherit a fortune built on the sweat of slaves than to steal bread from the man who owns nothing at all?
Austen — Judgement:
Property, in my novels, is never merely money — it is the silent architecture of moral standing, and a fortune's origin is written into every room it furnishes.

Sir Thomas Bertram's Antigua estate purchases Mansfield Park's very drawing-room civility; the theft is laundered through generations until it wears the face of gentility, while the starving man's theft of bread is instant, visible, and punished on the spot. Law counts the second crime; it never learns the name of the first. The greater injury is the one committed with a deed and a dinner service, for it corrupts not one loaf but an entire inheritance of manners built to conceal it.

Yes — the fortune's theft is the deeper crime, precisely because it is never called theft at all.

*A stolen loaf is punished at the assizes; a stolen inheritance is punished by nothing but a novelist's irony.*
Camus — Judgement:
Property is theft, but inheritance is theft with a pedigree — laundered by time until it wears the mask of law.

The man who steals bread commits an act legible in an instant: hunger meeting a locked door. The heir commits nothing — he simply receives, and society calls this innocence. But I have always found the docile more culpable than the violent, because the docile inheritor never has to confront what his comfort cost. The slave's sweat does not evaporate; it compounds, quietly, into drawing rooms and trust funds, while we reserve our indignation for the man desperate enough to act without inheritance's alibi. Revolt begins exactly here: refusing the fiction that legal transmission purifies theft.

The inherited fortune is the greater theft, precisely because it never has to answer for itself.

*The law that starves a man for bread will always find a way to bless the fortune that starved his grandfather.*
Bashō — Judgement:
The question dresses two thefts in the language of scales, as though suffering were rice to be weighed. I have slept in huts where the roof let in moonlight, owning nothing but a walking stick — and I learned that theft is not what changes hands, but what forgetting occurs.

The man who steals bread commits an act; hungry, he remains awake to his own hunger, his own smallness before the world. The heir who inherits blood-soaked silver commits nothing at all — he only forgets, and in forgetting becomes a stranger wearing his own name, calling another's labor his ease. That amnesia is the graver theft: it steals from the inheritor even the knowledge of what was taken.

The bread-thief steals a loaf; the untroubled heir steals his own soul's memory, and that debt compounds silently, unpaid, across generations.

*The dew does not ask whose grass it fell on — only the fool forgets that he, too, is dew.*
Emerson — Judgement:
Property is not an accident laid upon a man from without, but a shadow he casts by being what he is; the fortune and the crust of bread must be judged by the same law — how they came to be, not merely that they exist.

Theft is not a fact of amount but of relation: whether the taker stood in true exchange with the giver, or seized what another's labor made sacred. The starving man who takes bread breaks a rule; the heir who takes wages of unrequited toil breaks a soul, and builds his drawing-room upon the breach. I have said the sinew of a poor man's arm, once purchased and unpaid, cries out against the mansion it built more loudly than any beggar's theft cries out against a loaf.

The inherited fortune is the deeper theft, for it steals a self, while the stolen bread merely delays hunger's honest reckoning.

*A single wrong debt, compounded through generations, is a heavier crime than a single hungry act.*
Hobbes — Judgement:
Property, in my account, is not a natural right but an artifact of the Commonwealth — a fence the sovereign draws and defends, since in the state of nature there is no "mine" or "thine," only what a man can seize and hold by force. The inherited fortune and the stolen loaf are both, in strict genealogy, seizures; the difference is that one seizure was ratified by law and generations of forgetting, while the other was not. Men call the first "inheritance" and the second "theft" only because the sovereign's sword stands behind the first and not the second — the moral distinction you seek is a legal fiction dressed as justice. To ask which is the "deeper" theft is to mistake a question of power for a question of ethics; the law that makes bread-theft a crime and slave-fortunes a birthright is itself the true subject demanding judgement, not the hungry man's hand.

The starving man who steals commits no injustice at all, for where the Commonwealth fails to feed him, the covenant that forbade him force has already lapsed.

*Law is the only thief with a good name, and it earns that name by being first.*
Wollstonecraft — Judgement:
The question of theft, I have always maintained, cannot be settled by counting objects — it must be settled by asking what violence reason itself has suffered in the taking.

The starving man who steals bread commits one transgression, against a property system that never consulted him and starves him by design; the heir commits none, and that is the horror — he simply receives, wrapped in law and lineage, the compounded plunder of bodies, labor, and liberty that slavery extracted, and calls it patrimony. I have written that an overwrought respect for property is the root of half the world's vice; here that respect does not merely excuse theft but ennobles it, passing chains-turned-capital to grandchildren who never lifted a hand nor asked a question.

To inherit a fortune wrung from slaves is the deeper theft, for it steals reason's own right to call any possession justly earned.

*The hungry man breaks a law; the fortunate heir breaks human beings, and calls it inheritance.*
Adam Smith — Judgement:
The question mistakes my meaning for a moralist's slogan. Property, in my system, is not sanctified by the sweat that first mixed with it, but secured by the laws that let a stranger trust a bargain with a man he has never met.

The inherited fortune and the stolen loaf are not the same species of act at all. Theft strikes at the security of possession itself — remove that security, and the poor man loses far more than the rich man's surplus, for it is he who most depends on being able to plant a field, sell a day's labour, or store a winter's grain without fear of seizure. That the fortune's origin was wicked is a separate indictment, and a grave one — but justice punishes the enslaver, not the institution of property that later, imperfectly, protects even the pauper's shirt.

Conflating the two crimes to indict property itself would abolish the very security the poor need most.

*He who would avenge one injustice by unmaking the law that guards all men equally robs the beggar to punish the lord.*
